reasons: Scope is correct: Section 6.1 binds "the Company" (The Deerskin Companies), which is our party under the Company/Customer aliases, and it is a field-of-use restriction on our business; the drafter correctly declined to flag the reciprocal restriction on HDI in 6.3 as it benefits us.

Deviation classification is sound. The clause fails the fallback on material terms: scope extends beyond a named competing product to "products substantially similar to Deerskin Products" and "companies similar to Wilson's House of Leather and Excelled" (open-ended class), there is no internal-development or acquisition carve-out, and the auto-renewing one-year term in 4.1 means the term-only restriction can run indefinitely rather than being capped at 12 months. This is not a mere upgrade of an acceptable fallback.

Redline is actionable and directionally right: it deletes the open-ended "substantially similar"/"companies similar to" language, adds an express twelve-month cap measured from the Effective Date, and adds internal-development and acquisition carve-outs, while preserving HDI's exclusive "Deerskin" brand right — i.e., it lands on the stated fallback rather than over-reaching to outright deletion.

The 0.796 changed-character ratio is explained by excising the long parenthetical class of competitors; the substantive change is confined to the offending scope, duration and carve-out terms, so the edit is proportionate.

Comment is accurate, in the required tone and prefix, states the preferred position (deletion), explains the narrowing offered as fallback, and correctly notes HDI's rights under 6.1/6.3 are unaffected. Minor, non-disqualifying drafting caution: carve-outs (ii) and (iii) as worded (internal development of "any ... web site"; continuing to operate an acquired Internet apparel business) could be read to swallow the residual covenant, so expect counterparty pushback on qualifying them (e.g., excluding use of the "Deerskin" brand).
